title: De Gubernatione Dei
author: Salvian of Marseilles

passages.original: unde etiam illud mysticae auctoritatis exemplum, quo se non minus philosophum Maro probare uoluit quam.poetam, dicens: deum namque ire per omnes terrasque tractusque maris caelumque profundum. Tullius quoque: nec uero deus ipse, inquit, qui intellegitur a nobis, alio modois intellegi potest quam mens soluta quaedam et libera et segregata ab omni concretione mortali, omnia sentiens et mouens. alibi quoque nihil est inquit, praestantius deo: ab eo igitur mundum regi necesse est. nulli igitur naturae oboediens aut subiectus deus: omnem ergo regit ipse naturam: nisi forte nos uidelicet sapientissimi ita sentiamus, ut eum, a quo omnia regi dicimus, et regere simul et neglegere credamus.
passages.english: Hence too that example of mystic authority, by which Maro wished to prove himself no less a philosopher than a poet, when he says: "for God goes through all lands and the tracts of the sea and the deep heaven." Tullius also says: "Nor indeed can God himself, as he is understood by us, be understood in any other way than as a certain mind, unbound and free and separated from every mortal compound, perceiving and moving all things." Elsewhere too he says: "Nothing is more excellent than God; by him, therefore, the world must be governed." God, then, is obedient or subject to no nature; therefore he himself governs all nature. Unless perhaps we, most wise as we evidently are, should think in such a way as to believe that he by whom we say all things are governed both governs and neglects [them] at the same time.
passages.notes: Maro is Virgil (the quotation is from the Georgics); Tullius is Cicero. 'quam.poetam' read as 'quam poetam'; 'modois' read as 'modo'. 'nos uidelicet sapientissimi' is ironic.

passages.original: dicat mihi quisquis ille est, qui indignatur me ista dicere: numquid non sapientissimus omnium Socrates semper existimatus est, testimonio scilicet etiam Delfici daemonis, qui quasi princeps philosophorum sicut daemoniorum erat? uideamus ergo quas Socrates de pudicitia leges sanxerit et quas illi, de quibus loquimur. uxorem, inquit Socrates, propriam nullus habeat, matrimonia enim cunctis debent esse communia; sic namque maior erit concordia ciuitatum, si omnes uiri feminis sine discretione omnibus misceantur et omnes se scilicet feminae omnibus uiris sine distinctione substernant, ac si fiant omnes uiri omnium mulierum mariti, omnes feminae uirorum omnium uxores.
passages.english: Let whoever is indignant that I say these things tell me: was not Socrates always considered the wisest of all, by the testimony, of course, even of the Delphic demon, who was a sort of chief of philosophers just as [he was] of demons? Let us see, then, what laws Socrates established concerning chastity, and what laws those of whom we are speaking [established]. "Let no one," says Socrates, "have a wife of his own, for marriages ought to be common to all; for in this way the concord of cities will be greater, if all men have intercourse with all women without discrimination, and all women, of course, submit themselves to all men without distinction, and if all men become the husbands of all women, [and] all women the wives of all men."
passages.notes: The "Delphic demon" is the oracle of Apollo at Delphi, which declared Socrates the wisest of men; Salvian, as a Christian, calls the god a daemon. The community of wives described here is the proposal of Plato's Republic, which Salvian attributes to Socrates as its speaker.

passages.original: neo suffecit sapientissimo, ut quidam aiunt, philosopho docere hoc, nisi ipse fecisset; uxorem enim suam alteri uiro tradidit, scilicet sicut etiam Romanus Cato, id est alius Italiae Socrates. ecce quae sunt et Romanae et Atticae sapientiae exempla: omnes\' penitus maritos, quantum in ipsis fuit, lenones uxorum suarum esse fecerunt. sed uicit tamen Socrates, qui de hac re et libros condidit et memoriae haec pudenda mandauit.
passages.english: Nor was it enough for the philosopher, most wise as some call him, to teach this unless he had done it himself; for he handed over his own wife to another man, just as the Roman Cato also did, that is, the other Socrates of Italy. See what examples there are of both Roman and Attic wisdom: they made all husbands entirely, as far as lay in them, pimps of their own wives. But Socrates nevertheless won, since he both composed books on this matter and committed these shameful things to memory.
passages.notes: 'neo' read as 'nec'; stray mark after 'omnes' omitted. The philosopher is Socrates, to whom Salvian attributes the teaching of shared wives (from Plato's Republic). 'memoriae mandauit' may mean 'recorded in writing for posterity'.
